chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Khadir al-Nakha'i, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who has a debt due from another man, and the debtor denies it: He (the Imam) said, 'If the creditor swears an oath (from the debtor), he is not entitled to take anything from him; and if he leaves it (the denial) and does not swear an oath from him, then the creditor is upon his right (entitled to the debt).'

key_terms.اسْتَحْلَفَهُ: he demanded an oath from him

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling when a debtor denies a debt and the creditor chooses not to demand an oath?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the procedural mechanics of *qasam* (oath-taking) in debt disputes, emphasizing that the creditor's choice to demand an oath is a decisive act that, if accepted, extinguishes the debt. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the burden of proof initially lies with the claimant, but the specific mechanism of the debtor's oath serves as a legal substitute for proof when invoked. This ruling underscores the importance of procedural diligence in civil transactions, ensuring that rights are either formally secured through the oath or waived through inaction.
